name: Wyler
defunctReason: Wyler's innovative shock-resistant Incaflex technology couldn't save the brand from the quartz revolution and declining Swiss mechanical watch sales.
epitaph: Wyler made the unbreakable balance wheel — the Incaflex bent but never broke, unlike the company itself.
description: Wyler was a Swiss watch brand known for the patented Incaflex balance wheel — a flexible, shock-resistant design that was famously demonstrated by running over watches with cars. Based in Biel/Bienne, Wyler was a popular mid-century brand that faded after the quartz crisis.

keyCollections.name: Incaflex
keyCollections.description: Wyler's flagship line featuring the patented flexible alloy balance wheel that provided exceptional shock resistance, famously demonstrated by having cars drive over the watches.

keyCollections.name: Lifeguard
keyCollections.description: A robust diving and water-resistant collection designed for aquatic activities, featuring enhanced water protection and legible dials.

keyCollections.name: Heavy Duty
keyCollections.description: Professional-grade tool watches built for demanding environments, emphasising durability and reliability for industrial and military applications.

keyCollections.name: Dynawind
keyCollections.description: Automatic winding watches incorporating Wyler's self-winding technology with the Incaflex shock protection system.

timeline.event: Paul Wyler establishes the Wyler watch company in Biel/Bienne, Switzerland.
Wyler patents the revolutionary Incaflex balance wheel, a flexible alloy component providing superior shock resistance.
Wyler gains widespread recognition in the American market through dramatic demonstrations of watch durability, including the car-crushing publicity stunts.
The brand reaches peak popularity as a mid-priced Swiss watch known for reliability, competing successfully in the American market.
The quartz crisis begins to erode sales of mechanical Swiss watches, severely impacting Wyler's market position.
Wyler ceases operations, unable to recover from the prolonged effects of the quartz revolution on mid-range Swiss watchmaking.

faqItems.question: When did Wyler stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Wyler ceased production around 1990, having struggled for two decades following the quartz crisis that devastated many mid-range Swiss mechanical watch manufacturers.

faqItems.question: Are Wyler watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Vintage Wyler watches, particularly Incaflex models and early diving watches, hold modest collector value. They represent an important chapter in shock-resistant technology and appeal to collectors interested in mid-century American market Swiss watches.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Wyler watch today?
faqItems.answer: Original Wyler watches are only available through the vintage market, including auction houses, specialist dealers, and online platforms. The brand has not been revived for new production.

faqItems.question: What made the Incaflex technology special?
faqItems.answer: The Incaflex balance wheel used a patented flexible alloy that could absorb shocks without damage, a significant innovation when watches were far more vulnerable to impact. Wyler famously proved this by having vehicles drive over their watches in public demonstrations.

faqItems.question: Was Wyler a luxury brand?
faqItems.answer: Wyler positioned itself in the mid-range market, offering Swiss quality and innovative technology at accessible prices. It was particularly popular in the United States as a reliable, durable everyday watch rather than a prestige timepiece.

name: Moeris
defunctReason: Moeris was absorbed into the SSIH group and effectively ceased to exist as an independent brand during the restructuring that created the Swatch Group.
epitaph: Saint-Imier's quiet craftsman — Moeris made alarm watches that woke you gently, then was itself put to sleep by corporate consolidation.
description: Moeris was a Swiss watch manufacturer from Saint-Imier, founded in 1893. Part of the SSIH group, Moeris was known for alarm watches and solid mid-range timepieces before being absorbed during the creation of the Swatch Group.

keyCollections.name: Alarm
keyCollections.description: Mechanical alarm wristwatches that became Moeris's signature product, featuring reliable cricket-style movements that competed with the likes of Vulcain and Jaeger-LeCoultre.

keyCollections.name: Pointer Date
keyCollections.description: Elegant dress watches featuring a centre-mounted date hand pointing to numerals around the dial periphery, popular throughout the 1950s and 1960s.

keyCollections.name: Chronograph
keyCollections.description: Sporting chronographs produced during the mid-twentieth century, typically featuring two-register layouts with reliable hand-wound movements.

keyCollections.name: Military
keyCollections.description: Robust field watches supplied to various armed forces, characterised by luminous hands, clear legibility and durable cases built for active service.

timeline.event: Henri Blanc establishes Moeris in Saint-Imier, Switzerland, initially producing pocket watches.
Moeris transitions to wristwatch production and develops its first alarm calibres, establishing a market niche.
The brand gains recognition for its Pointer Date models and expands exports to European and Asian markets.
Moeris becomes part of SSIH (Société Suisse pour l'Industrie Horlogère), joining the conglomerate alongside Omega and Tissot.
Following the merger of SSIH and ASUAG to form the Swatch Group, Moeris ceases independent production and the brand becomes dormant.

faqItems.question: When did Moeris stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Moeris effectively ceased production in 1983 when SSIH merged with ASUAG to create the Swatch Group, and the brand was discontinued during the subsequent rationalisation of marques.

faqItems.question: Are Moeris watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Vintage Moeris timepieces, particularly the alarm watches and chronographs, hold modest collector value. Well-preserved examples with original dials and functioning alarm complications command higher prices among enthusiasts of mid-century Swiss watchmaking.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Moeris watch today?
faqItems.answer: Moeris watches are only available on the secondary market through vintage dealers, auction houses and online platforms. No new production has occurred since the brand's absorption into the Swatch Group.

faqItems.question: What was Moeris best known for?
faqItems.answer: Moeris earned its reputation primarily for mechanical alarm wristwatches, offering a more accessible alternative to premium alarm watches from Vulcain or Jaeger-LeCoultre whilst maintaining Swiss quality standards.

faqItems.question: Where were Moeris watches made?
faqItems.answer: All Moeris watches were manufactured in Saint-Imier, a traditional watchmaking town in the Bernese Jura region of Switzerland, home to several historic horological firms.

name: Election
defunctReason: Election gradually faded after the quartz crisis, unable to rebuild its identity in the post-crisis luxury watch landscape.
epitaph: A century of Swiss precision that the electorate of collectors has largely forgotten — Election's Grand Prix movements deserved better.
description: Election was a Swiss watch brand from La Chaux-de-Fonds, founded in 1892. Known for chronometer-grade movements and winning multiple observatory prizes, Election produced quality timepieces for over a century before the quartz crisis sealed its fate.

keyCollections.name: Grand Prix
keyCollections.description: Election's flagship collection celebrating the brand's numerous chronometry competition victories and observatory prizes, featuring precision-certified movements.

keyCollections.name: Doublematic
keyCollections.description: A technically accomplished automatic watch featuring both day and date complications, representative of Election's mid-century mechanical expertise.

keyCollections.name: Election Chronograph
keyCollections.description: Sporty chronograph models produced primarily during the 1960s and 1970s, often housing reliable Valjoux or Landeron movements.

keyCollections.name: Election Automatic
keyCollections.description: Core collection of self-winding watches that formed the backbone of Election's catalogue from the 1950s onwards, known for reliable timekeeping at accessible price points.

timeline.event: Election founded in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, entering the competitive Swiss watchmaking industry.
The brand establishes its reputation for precision timekeeping, beginning to compete in Swiss observatory chronometer trials.
Post-war expansion sees Election develop its automatic movement range and gain distribution across European and Latin American markets.
The quartz crisis begins, severely impacting Election's traditional mechanical watch production and market position.
Election struggles to adapt to the changed market landscape, significantly reducing its product range and workforce.
Election ceases production, ending over a century of Swiss watchmaking after failing to recover from the quartz crisis.

faqItems.question: When did Election stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Election ceased production in 1995 after gradually declining throughout the 1980s. The brand never recovered from the quartz crisis that devastated traditional Swiss mechanical watchmaking in the 1970s.

faqItems.question: Are Election watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Vintage Election watches hold modest value among collectors, particularly chronograph models and pieces with documented chronometer certifications. Their observatory prize-winning heritage adds historical interest, though prices remain accessible compared to better-known Swiss brands.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy an Election watch today?
faqItems.answer: New Election watches are no longer available as the brand is defunct. However, vintage Election timepieces regularly appear on secondary markets, auction houses, and specialist vintage watch dealers.

faqItems.question: What made Election watches notable?
faqItems.answer: Election distinguished itself through chronometer-grade movements and multiple observatory competition victories. The brand was recognised for producing precision timepieces that competed successfully against established Swiss manufacturers in accuracy trials.

faqItems.question: Where were Election watches sold?
faqItems.answer: Election had strong distribution networks across Europe and particularly in Latin American markets, where the brand developed a loyal following throughout the mid-twentieth century.

graveyardStory.rise: Election built its name in La Chaux-de-Fonds as a precision-focused Swiss brand, earning attention for chronometer-grade movements and observatory-prize heritage.
graveyardStory.whatTheyMade: The brand made refined mechanical wristwatches including Grand Prix precision models, Doublematic day-date watches, chronographs, and automatic everyday watches.
graveyardStory.whyDisappeared: Election was weakened by the quartz crisis and never rebuilt a distinctive post-crisis identity. Production narrowed through the 1980s before the brand faded out in the 1990s.
graveyardStory.collectorInterest: Collectors look for Election chronographs, chronometer-linked pieces, and clean automatic models; the brand is historically interesting but still undervalued against better-known Swiss precision makers.

name: Wittnauer
defunctReason: Wittnauer was gradually absorbed into the Bulova brand family after Bulova's acquisition by Citizen, losing its independent identity by the early 2000s.
epitaph: Wittnauer timed Lindbergh's Atlantic crossing and Byrd's polar flights — aviation history written in Swiss-American collaboration.
description: Wittnauer was a Swiss-American watch brand, originally the US distribution arm of Longines, founded by Albert Wittnauer in 1880. Known for chronographs used in aviation milestones including Lindbergh's transatlantic flight. The brand was absorbed into the Bulova family.

keyCollections.name: Professional Chronograph
keyCollections.description: Wittnauer's flagship chronograph line, renowned for reliability and used extensively by aviators and professionals throughout the mid-20th century.

keyCollections.name: All-Proof
keyCollections.description: A rugged, water-resistant collection developed in partnership with Longines, marketed for durability in demanding conditions.

keyCollections.name: Genève
keyCollections.description: An elegant dress watch collection emphasising Swiss craftsmanship, positioned as an accessible luxury line for the American market.

keyCollections.name: Electronic
keyCollections.description: Wittnauer's range of tuning fork and early quartz watches from the 1960s and 1970s, reflecting the brand's embrace of emerging technology.

timeline.event: Albert Wittnauer, a Swiss immigrant, establishes A. Wittnauer Co. in New York City as the American distribution agent for Longines watches.
Wittnauer-Longines timepieces accompany Charles Lindbergh on his historic solo transatlantic flight, enhancing the brand's aviation credentials.
Admiral Richard E. Byrd uses Wittnauer chronometers during his Antarctic expeditions, cementing the brand's reputation for precision timing.
The Longines-Wittnauer Watch Company is formally established as a consolidated American subsidiary.
Wittnauer becomes part of the Bulova Corporation following corporate restructuring within the Longines-Wittnauer group.
Following Citizen's acquisition of Bulova, the Wittnauer brand is phased out as a distinct watchmaking identity.

faqItems.question: When did Wittnauer stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Wittnauer effectively ceased independent production around 2002, after the brand was absorbed into the Bulova family following Citizen's acquisition. The name was occasionally licensed thereafter but no longer represented active watchmaking.

faqItems.question: Are Wittnauer watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Vintage Wittnauer watches, particularly the Professional Chronographs from the 1960s and aviation-related pieces, are sought after by collectors. Their historical significance and quality Swiss movements contribute to enduring value in the secondary market.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Wittnauer watch today?
faqItems.answer: Original Wittnauer watches are only available on the vintage and pre-owned market. The brand name has occasionally appeared on licensed products, but these do not represent the heritage Swiss-American manufacturing of the original company.

faqItems.question: What is the connection between Wittnauer and Longines?
faqItems.answer: Albert Wittnauer established his company as the exclusive American distributor for Longines in 1880. The two brands operated closely for decades under the Longines-Wittnauer Watch Company, sharing movements and distribution networks until corporate changes in the 1970s separated them.

faqItems.question: Were Wittnauer watches used in aviation history?
faqItems.answer: Yes, Wittnauer-Longines timepieces were famously worn by Charles Lindbergh during his 1927 transatlantic flight and by Admiral Richard Byrd on Antarctic expeditions, establishing the brand's strong association with aviation and exploration.

name: Revue Thommen
defunctReason: Revue Thommen's parent company Grovana went bankrupt, and the brand ceased production after failing to find sustainable new ownership.
epitaph: Waldenburg's aviator — Revue Thommen put altimeters in cockpits and chronographs on pilot wrists for over 160 years.
description: Revue Thommen was a Swiss watch and instrument maker from Waldenburg, founded in 1853. Famous for aviation instruments and the Airspeed line of pilot watches, the brand was also known for producing alarm calibres used across the industry.

keyCollections.name: Airspeed
keyCollections.description: Aviation-inspired pilot watches drawing upon Revue Thommen's expertise in aircraft instrumentation, featuring legible dials and robust construction.

keyCollections.name: Cricket
keyCollections.description: Mechanical alarm watches utilising the brand's renowned in-house alarm calibres, which were also supplied to other prestigious manufacturers.

keyCollections.name: Diver Professional
keyCollections.description: Purpose-built diving watches offering substantial water resistance and professional-grade specifications for underwater use.

keyCollections.name: Classic
keyCollections.description: Traditional dress watches emphasising clean aesthetics and Swiss mechanical craftsmanship in a more formal presentation.

timeline.event: Gédéon Thommen established a watch components factory in Waldenburg, Switzerland.
The company began manufacturing complete pocket watches under its own name.
Revue Thommen commenced production of aircraft instruments, establishing its aviation heritage.
Introduced mechanical alarm calibres that would become widely adopted throughout the Swiss watch industry.
The brand was acquired by Grovana Watch Company, relocating production within Switzerland.
Parent company Grovana declared bankruptcy, leading to the cessation of Revue Thommen watch production.

faqItems.question: When did Revue Thommen stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Revue Thommen ceased watch production in 2015 when its parent company, Grovana Watch Company, went bankrupt. The brand had been under Grovana's ownership since 2002.

faqItems.question: Are Revue Thommen watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Vintage Revue Thommen watches retain collector interest, particularly models featuring the brand's acclaimed alarm movements and aviation-themed Airspeed pieces. Their value lies in solid Swiss engineering and the brand's historical significance in alarm calibre production.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Revue Thommen watch today?
faqItems.answer: New Revue Thommen watches are no longer manufactured, but pre-owned examples regularly appear on secondary markets and auction platforms. The Airspeed and Cricket alarm models remain the most sought-after.

faqItems.question: What made Revue Thommen's alarm movements special?
faqItems.answer: Revue Thommen developed highly regarded mechanical alarm calibres that were not only used in their own Cricket watches but were supplied to other prestigious Swiss brands, demonstrating the technical excellence of their movement production.

faqItems.question: Did Revue Thommen only make watches?
faqItems.answer: No, the company was also a significant manufacturer of aviation instruments from 1936 onwards. This expertise in aircraft instrumentation directly influenced their Airspeed watch collection and enhanced the brand's credibility among aviation enthusiasts.

name: Solvil et Titus
defunctReason: After being acquired by City Chain (Stelux Group) in Hong Kong, Solvil et Titus was repositioned as a fashion brand and lost its horological identity entirely.
epitaph: A Swiss chronograph house that conquered Asia, then was consumed by it — Solvil et Titus became a ghost haunting Hong Kong malls.
description: Solvil et Titus was a respected Swiss watch brand founded in 1887, known for quality chronographs and calendar watches. Enormously popular in Asia, the brand was acquired by Hong Kong's Stelux Group and repositioned as a fashion brand, losing its Swiss horological heritage.

keyCollections.name: Solvil Chronograph
keyCollections.description: High-quality manual-wound chronographs produced during the brand's Swiss manufacturing era, some featuring panda dials that have become collectible.

keyCollections.name: Pandat Chronograph
keyCollections.description: Distinctive chronograph series featuring contrasting subdials, popular among vintage collectors for their resemblance to sought-after Paul Newman Daytona aesthetics.

keyCollections.name: Calendar
keyCollections.description: Triple calendar and complete calendar watches that demonstrated the brand's mechanical competence during the mid-twentieth century.

keyCollections.name: Solvil Dress Watches
keyCollections.description: Elegant thin-cased timepieces produced for the Asian market, representing the brand's transition toward accessible luxury.

timeline.event: Paul Ditisheim establishes Solvil in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, focusing on precision timekeeping.
Solvil merges with Titus to form Solvil et Titus, combining manufacturing strengths and expanding distribution.
The brand achieves significant popularity in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong, becoming one of the most recognised Swiss names in the region.
Hong Kong's Stelux Holdings acquires Solvil et Titus, beginning the shift toward Asian market focus.
Memorable advertising campaigns in Asia cement the brand's romantic image, particularly in Hong Kong and Taiwan.
Swiss manufacturing ceases as Solvil et Titus is fully repositioned as a fashion-oriented brand under Stelux Group.

faqItems.question: When did Solvil et Titus stop making watches in Switzerland?
faqItems.answer: Solvil et Titus ceased Swiss horological production around 2000, when parent company Stelux Group fully transitioned the brand to fashion-oriented manufacturing outside Switzerland.

faqItems.question: Are vintage Solvil et Titus watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Pre-1970s Solvil et Titus chronographs and calendar watches retain collector interest, particularly models with Valjoux movements. The Pandat chronographs command premiums due to their aesthetic similarity to Paul Newman Daytonas.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Solvil et Titus watch today?
faqItems.answer: The brand continues under Stelux Group's City Chain retail network, primarily selling fashion quartz watches in Asia. These bear no connection to the original Swiss horological tradition.

faqItems.question: Who originally founded Solvil et Titus?
faqItems.answer: Paul Ditisheim, a respected Swiss chronometer maker, founded Solvil in 1887. The Titus name was added following a 1930 merger, creating the combined Solvil et Titus brand.

faqItems.question: Why are Solvil et Titus Paul Newman chronographs collectible?
faqItems.answer: Certain 1960s Solvil chronographs feature exotic panda dials and Art Deco-inspired registers that closely resemble the famous Paul Newman Rolex Daytona dials, making them attractive alternatives for collectors.

name: Ollech & Wajs
defunctReason: Ollech & Wajs, a Zurich-based maker of professional dive watches, gradually ceased production as its founding partners retired and the quartz crisis had already eroded its market.
epitaph: Zurich's deepest secret — Ollech & Wajs built dive watches for professionals who needed function over fashion.
description: Ollech & Wajs was a Swiss dive watch specialist founded in 1956 in Zurich, producing robust professional diving instruments. Known for their Caribbean 1000 series and no-frills approach to tool watches.

keyCollections.name: Caribbean 1000
keyCollections.description: The brand's flagship professional dive watch rated to 1000 metres, featuring a robust case design and exceptional water resistance for serious diving applications.

keyCollections.name: M-4 Diver
keyCollections.description: A military-specification dive watch produced for professional and armed forces use, characterised by its utilitarian design and reliable automatic movement.

keyCollections.name: OW Precision
keyCollections.description: A range of precision-focused timepieces demonstrating the brand's commitment to accuracy alongside their diving credentials.

timeline.event: Albert Ollech and Jorge Wajs founded the company in Zurich, initially focusing on assembling and distributing professional-grade diving watches.
Introduced the Caribbean 1000, establishing the brand's reputation for extreme depth-rated professional dive watches.
Expanded distribution across Europe and North America, gaining recognition among professional divers and military personnel.
The quartz crisis severely impacted sales, though the brand maintained a loyal following among dive watch enthusiasts.
Production ceased as the founding partners retired, marking the end of nearly fifty years of Swiss dive watch manufacturing.

faqItems.question: When did Ollech & Wajs stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Ollech & Wajs ceased production around 2005 when the founding partners, Albert Ollech and Jorge Wajs, retired from the business after nearly fifty years of watchmaking.

faqItems.question: Are Ollech & Wajs watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Vintage Ollech & Wajs dive watches, particularly the Caribbean 1000 series, have developed a cult following among collectors who appreciate their professional specifications and no-nonsense tool watch approach, commanding respectable prices on the secondary market.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy an Ollech & Wajs watch today?
faqItems.answer: As the brand is defunct, Ollech & Wajs watches are only available through the vintage and pre-owned market, with examples appearing at specialist watch dealers and auction platforms.

faqItems.question: What made Ollech & Wajs dive watches special?
faqItems.answer: The brand earned respect for producing genuinely professional diving instruments with exceptional depth ratings, particularly the Caribbean 1000 with its 1000-metre water resistance, at prices accessible to working divers rather than collectors.

faqItems.question: Were Ollech & Wajs watches used by military forces?
faqItems.answer: Yes, various military and professional diving units utilised Ollech & Wajs timepieces, appreciating their robust construction, reliable movements, and legible dials designed for demanding underwater conditions.

name: LIP
defunctReason: After a famous worker self-management experiment following bankruptcy in 1973, LIP finally closed in 1977, a symbol of French industrial decline and worker resistance.
revivalAttempt: The brand name was licensed and watches are sold under the LIP name, but as a fashion/heritage brand without the original manufacture.
epitaph: The workers of Besançon seized the factory and made watches without bosses — LIP became France's most political timepiece.
description: LIP was France's most iconic watch brand, founded in 1867 in Besançon. Famous for producing the electronic R27 watch given to world leaders including de Gaulle and Churchill. The 1973 LIP affair — when workers occupied the factory and self-managed production — became a landmark in French labour history.

keyCollections.name: Electronic R27
keyCollections.description: France's first electronic watch, launched in 1952, presented to dignitaries including General de Gaulle, Winston Churchill, and Dwight Eisenhower as diplomatic gifts representing French technological achievement.

keyCollections.name: Nautic-Ski
keyCollections.description: A highly regarded diver's chronograph introduced in the 1960s, known for its robust construction and distinctive French styling, becoming a cult collector's piece.

keyCollections.name: Himalaya
keyCollections.description: A rugged tool watch designed for extreme conditions, reflecting LIP's commitment to functional timepieces for professional use.

keyCollections.name: Mach 2000
keyCollections.description: A futuristic design collaboration with designer Roger Tallon in the 1970s, featuring bold geometric cases that became icons of French industrial design.

timeline.event: Emmanuel Lipmann establishes a watchmaking workshop in Besançon, France's traditional watchmaking capital.
The company officially adopts the name LIP, derived from the founder's surname.
LIP launches the Electronic R27, France's first electronic watch, marking a major technological achievement.
Following bankruptcy, workers occupy the factory and resume production under self-management, creating the famous 'LIP Affair' that captivated France.
The original LIP manufacture closes definitively after the failure of various rescue attempts, ending over a century of French watchmaking.
The LIP brand is relaunched under licence, producing heritage-inspired watches manufactured outside the original facility.

faqItems.question: When did LIP stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: The original LIP manufacture ceased operations in 1977 after a prolonged financial crisis, though the brand name has since been licensed and revived for heritage-style watches.

faqItems.question: Are LIP watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Vintage LIP watches, particularly the Electronic R27, Nautic-Ski chronographs, and Mach 2000 designs, are increasingly sought after by collectors of French horology and mid-century design.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a LIP watch today?
faqItems.answer: Yes, watches bearing the LIP name are currently available through licensed production, offering designs inspired by the brand's historic models, though these are not produced in the original Besançon manufacture.

faqItems.question: What was the LIP Affair?
faqItems.answer: The LIP Affair of 1973 was a landmark event in French labour history when workers occupied their factory following bankruptcy, self-managing production and sales of watches, becoming a powerful symbol of worker resistance.

faqItems.question: Which famous people received LIP watches?
faqItems.answer: LIP's Electronic R27 was presented as a symbol of French innovation to General de Gaulle, Winston Churchill, Dwight Eisenhower, and other world leaders during the 1950s and 1960s.

name: Dubey & Schaldenbrand
defunctReason: Dubey & Schaldenbrand struggled for decades with ownership changes and eventually ceased production around 2014 after failing to establish a viable market position.
epitaph: The split-seconds specialists of La Chaux-de-Fonds — Dubey & Schaldenbrand made rattrapantes affordable before affordable was fashionable.
description: Dubey & Schaldenbrand was a Swiss watchmaker founded in 1946 in La Chaux-de-Fonds, specialising in split-seconds chronographs and complications at accessible price points. The brand went through multiple ownership changes before ceasing production.

keyCollections.name: Spiral
keyCollections.description: The brand's signature collection featuring distinctive spiral-shaped cases, representing their most recognisable and avant-garde design language.

keyCollections.name: Aerodyn
keyCollections.description: A collection characterised by aerodynamic case designs with flowing lines, including the notable Aerodyn Duo featuring dual time zones.

keyCollections.name: Index
keyCollections.description: Classic dress watch collection including complications such as the Réserve de Marche power reserve indicator, aimed at traditional watch enthusiasts.

keyCollections.name: Grand Dôme
keyCollections.description: Collection featuring prominently domed crystals and vintage-inspired aesthetics, paying homage to 1940s watchmaking design.

timeline.event: Georges Dubey and René Schaldenbrand founded the company in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, initially focusing on complicated timepieces.
The brand gained recognition for producing affordable split-seconds chronographs, a complication typically reserved for high-end manufacturers.
Cinette Robert acquired the dormant brand and relaunched it with distinctive designs including the spiral-cased models.
The company changed hands again, with new ownership attempting to reposition the brand in the competitive Swiss watch market.
Dubey & Schaldenbrand ceased production after failing to establish a sustainable market position following years of ownership instability.

faqItems.question: When did Dubey & Schaldenbrand stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Dubey & Schaldenbrand ceased watch production around 2014, following decades of ownership changes and struggles to maintain a viable market presence in the competitive Swiss watch industry.

faqItems.question: Are Dubey & Schaldenbrand watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Dubey & Schaldenbrand watches retain modest collector interest, particularly the distinctive Spiral collection and their split-seconds chronographs. Values remain relatively accessible compared to mainstream Swiss brands, though pristine examples of unusual models command premiums.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Dubey & Schaldenbrand watch today?
faqItems.answer: New Dubey & Schaldenbrand watches are no longer available as the brand ceased production in 2014. Pre-owned examples can be found through specialist dealers, auction houses, and online marketplaces at reasonable prices.

faqItems.question: What made Dubey & Schaldenbrand watches distinctive?
faqItems.answer: The brand was known for offering complicated movements, particularly split-seconds chronographs, at more accessible price points than competitors. Under Cinette Robert's ownership from 1995, they also became recognised for unconventional case designs, most notably the spiral-shaped cases.

faqItems.question: Who designed the iconic Spiral watches?
faqItems.answer: The distinctive Spiral collection was developed following Cinette Robert's acquisition of the brand in 1995, representing a bold departure from traditional Swiss watch design with its sculptural, spiral-shaped cases.

name: Mimo (Girard-Perregaux)
defunctReason: Mimo was phased out by Girard-Perregaux as the parent company consolidated its brand portfolio in the late 1960s.
epitaph: Girard-Perregaux's second label — Mimo put La Chaux-de-Fonds movements on modest wrists before being quietly retired.
description: Mimo was a secondary brand of Girard-Perregaux, used for more accessible watches from the 1920s to 1970s. Known for alarm watches (Mimolarm) and simple, well-made timepieces using GP movements.

keyCollections.name: Mimolarm
keyCollections.description: Mimo's signature alarm watch featuring a mechanical alarm complication, produced from the 1950s onwards and offering accessible alarm functionality using Girard-Perregaux calibres.

keyCollections.name: Chronostop
keyCollections.description: A practical chronograph line offering timing functions at a more accessible price point than mainline Girard-Perregaux chronographs.

keyCollections.name: Automatic Calendar
keyCollections.description: Dependable automatic watches featuring date complications, representing Mimo's everyday dress watch offerings with reliable GP-derived movements.

timeline.event: Mimo established as a secondary brand by Girard-Perregaux to offer more affordable Swiss timepieces.
Introduction of the Mimolarm, a mechanical alarm watch that became the brand's most recognised product line.
Mimo expands its catalogue with automatic and calendar complications, maintaining its position as GP's accessible offering.
Mimo discontinued as Girard-Perregaux consolidates its brand portfolio, focusing resources on its primary marque.

faqItems.question: When did Mimo stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Mimo ceased production around 1970 when parent company Girard-Perregaux decided to consolidate its brand portfolio and focus exclusively on its primary namesake brand.

faqItems.question: Are Mimo watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Mimo watches hold modest value in the vintage market, with the Mimolarm alarm watches commanding the most collector interest due to their reliable alarm complication and connection to Girard-Perregaux craftsmanship.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Mimo watch today?
faqItems.answer: Mimo watches are only available on the secondary market through vintage watch dealers, auction houses, and online platforms. The brand has not been revived since its discontinuation.

faqItems.question: What is the relationship between Mimo and Girard-Perregaux?
faqItems.answer: Mimo was a subsidiary brand created by Girard-Perregaux to offer more accessible Swiss watches. The watches often utilised GP movements and manufacturing expertise but were positioned at lower price points.

faqItems.question: What movements did Mimo watches use?
faqItems.answer: Mimo watches typically employed movements derived from or manufactured by Girard-Perregaux, ensuring Swiss quality whilst maintaining competitive pricing for the secondary brand.

name: Paul Ditisheim
defunctReason: Paul Ditisheim's workshop was absorbed into larger groups after decades of producing observatory prize-winning chronometers, as the market for artisanal precision timekeeping vanished.
epitaph: The man who won more observatory prizes than anyone — Paul Ditisheim's chronometers were the most accurate watches on Earth, and almost no one remembers.
description: Paul Ditisheim was a legendary Swiss chronometer maker from La Chaux-de-Fonds who won more observatory prizes for precision than any contemporary. His chronometers set accuracy records and he founded the Solvil brand. His work represents the pinnacle of mechanical precision.

keyCollections.name: Solvil Chronometer
keyCollections.description: The flagship precision chronometers that bore the Solvil name, established in 1914, representing Ditisheim's commercial line of observatory-grade timekeepers.

keyCollections.name: Observatory Prize Chronometers
keyCollections.description: Exceptional precision instruments submitted to Swiss observatory trials, winning numerous first prizes at Neuchâtel, Geneva, and Kew observatories throughout the early twentieth century.

keyCollections.name: Marine Chronometers
keyCollections.description: Deck watches and marine chronometers produced for naval navigation, embodying the highest standards of mechanical accuracy.

keyCollections.name: Solvil et Titus
keyCollections.description: The merged brand combining Ditisheim's Solvil with the Titus name, producing quality timepieces for international markets from 1930 onwards.

timeline.event: Paul Ditisheim established his chronometer workshop in La Chaux-de-Fonds, beginning a career dedicated to precision timekeeping.
Won first prize at the Neuchâtel Observatory trials, beginning an unprecedented streak of accuracy awards.
Founded the Solvil brand as a commercial vehicle for his precision chronometers.
Solvil merged with Titus to form Solvil et Titus, expanding distribution particularly in Asian markets.
Paul Ditisheim passed away, leaving behind a legacy of over 200 observatory prizes for chronometric excellence.
The original Paul Ditisheim workshop ceased independent operations, absorbed into the broader Solvil et Titus organisation.

faqItems.question: When did Paul Ditisheim stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: The independent Paul Ditisheim workshop ceased operations around 1960, though the Solvil et Titus brand he helped create continued production under different ownership.

faqItems.question: Are Paul Ditisheim watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Authentic Paul Ditisheim chronometers, particularly those with observatory prize provenance, are highly prized by collectors of precision horology and can command significant prices at auction.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Paul Ditisheim watch today?
faqItems.answer: Original Paul Ditisheim timepieces are only available through vintage dealers, auction houses, and private collectors, as the brand no longer produces watches.

faqItems.question: Why was Paul Ditisheim so renowned for precision?
faqItems.answer: Ditisheim won over 200 observatory prizes for chronometric accuracy during his career, more than any contemporary watchmaker, and his instruments repeatedly set records at the Neuchâtel, Geneva, and Kew observatories.

faqItems.question: What is the connection between Paul Ditisheim and Solvil et Titus?
faqItems.answer: Paul Ditisheim founded the Solvil brand in 1914, which later merged with Titus in 1930 to form Solvil et Titus, a company that continues to operate today primarily in Asian markets.

name: Minerva
defunctReason: Minerva was acquired by Richemont in 2006 and absorbed into Montblanc. The Minerva brand name was retired; the Villeret manufacture now produces movements exclusively for Montblanc.
epitaph: The Villeret chronograph masters whose calibres outperformed their fame — Minerva now beats inside Montblanc, unnamed.
description: Minerva was a Swiss movement manufacturer founded in 1858 in Villeret, renowned for producing some of the finest chronograph calibres ever made. The manufacture was acquired by Richemont and integrated into Montblanc, which continues to use Minerva movements in its high-end pieces.

keyCollections.name: Pythagore
keyCollections.description: A refined dress watch collection showcasing Minerva's expertise in slim, elegant timepieces with exceptional finishing and classical proportions.

keyCollections.name: Chronograph Series
keyCollections.description: Minerva's celebrated chronograph watches, housing the legendary Calibre 13-20 and its derivatives, regarded among the finest hand-wound chronograph movements ever produced.

keyCollections.name: Military Chronographs
keyCollections.description: Robust timing instruments supplied to various armed forces throughout the 20th century, prized for their legibility, accuracy, and durability under demanding conditions.

keyCollections.name: Stopwatch & Timer Instruments
keyCollections.description: Professional timing devices including the renowned Calibre 48 stopwatch movement, used extensively in sports timing and scientific applications.

timeline.event: Charles-Yvan Robert establishes a watchmaking workshop in Villeret, in the Bernese Jura region of Switzerland.
The company adopts the Minerva name, referencing the Roman goddess of wisdom and craftsmanship.
Minerva introduces the legendary Calibre 13-20 chronograph movement, establishing the manufacture's reputation for horological excellence.
The Calibre 48 stopwatch movement is launched, becoming an industry standard for professional timing applications.
Richemont acquires Minerva and integrates the Villeret manufacture into Montblanc's watchmaking operations.
The Minerva brand is formally retired; the manufacture continues producing high-end movements exclusively under the Montblanc name.

faqItems.question: When did Minerva stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Minerva ceased producing watches under its own name in 2007, following its acquisition by Richemont in 2006. The Villeret manufacture was absorbed into Montblanc, which now uses Minerva movements in its prestige collections.

faqItems.question: Are Minerva watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Vintage Minerva timepieces, particularly chronographs fitted with the Calibre 13-20 and its variants, are highly sought after by collectors. Their exceptional movement quality and historical significance command strong prices at auction.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Minerva watch today?
faqItems.answer: Original Minerva-branded watches are only available on the secondary market through specialist dealers and auction houses. However, the Minerva manufacture continues producing movements for Montblanc's 1858 and Heritage collections.

faqItems.question: What made Minerva chronograph movements so special?
faqItems.answer: Minerva's chronograph calibres, particularly the 13-20, were celebrated for their horizontal coupling, column-wheel construction, and exceptional hand-finishing. The movements offered precise timing with beautifully executed traditional techniques.

faqItems.question: What is the connection between Minerva and Montblanc?
faqItems.answer: Montblanc acquired Minerva through Richemont in 2006. The Villeret manufacture now produces high-complication movements for Montblanc's premium watch lines, preserving Minerva's technical heritage under a different brand name.

name: Tavannes Watch Co
defunctReason: Once one of Switzerland's largest watch producers, Tavannes was gradually absorbed into the Cyma brand and the broader SSIH group, losing its independent identity by the mid-1960s.
epitaph: One of Switzerland's biggest names became one of its most forgotten — Tavannes made millions of watches before vanishing into corporate alphabet soup.
description: Tavannes Watch Co was one of the largest Swiss watch manufacturers of the early 20th century, producing millions of watches from its Jura Mountain factory. The brand became intertwined with Cyma and was eventually absorbed into the SSIH group.

keyCollections.name: Tavannes Chronograph
keyCollections.description: Highly regarded vintage chronographs produced from the 1930s through 1950s, featuring reliable in-house movements and clean dial designs favoured by collectors today.

keyCollections.name: Golfer
keyCollections.description: A distinctive sports watch from the 1950s featuring a rotating bezel for timing golf rounds, representing the brand's innovation in purpose-built timepieces.

keyCollections.name: La Captive
keyCollections.description: An elegant Art Deco ladies' watch from the 1920s-30s, showcasing the brand's expertise in decorative women's timepieces during the interwar period.

keyCollections.name: Military Watches
keyCollections.description: Robust field watches supplied to various armed forces during both World Wars, cementing Tavannes' reputation for reliable, accurate timekeeping under demanding conditions.

timeline.event: Henri-Frédéric Sandoz establishes Tavannes Watch Co in the village of Tavannes in the Bernese Jura mountains.
Tavannes merges with Cyma, forming a powerful Swiss watchmaking alliance whilst both brands retain their separate identities.
At its peak, the combined Tavannes-Cyma operation becomes one of Switzerland's largest watch manufacturers, producing over one million watches annually.
Becomes part of SSIH (Société Suisse pour l'Industrie Horlogère), joining Omega and Tissot in the watchmaking conglomerate.
Tavannes ceases to exist as an independent brand, fully absorbed into SSIH's operations with production consolidated under the Cyma name.

faqItems.question: When did Tavannes stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Tavannes ceased independent production around 1966, when the brand was fully absorbed into the SSIH group structure and its identity merged with sister brand Cyma.

faqItems.question: Are Tavannes watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Vintage Tavannes watches, particularly chronographs from the 1940s and 1950s, are increasingly sought after by collectors for their quality movements and historical significance as products of one of Switzerland's largest pre-war manufacturers.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Tavannes watch today?
faqItems.answer: Tavannes watches are only available through the vintage market, with no new production. Collectors can find examples at specialist dealers, auction houses, and online marketplaces, with prices varying according to model, condition, and rarity.

faqItems.question: What is the connection between Tavannes and Cyma?
faqItems.answer: Tavannes and Cyma merged in 1908, sharing manufacturing facilities and movements whilst maintaining separate brand identities until the 1960s when Tavannes was discontinued and absorbed into Cyma.

faqItems.question: Did Tavannes make military watches?
faqItems.answer: Yes, Tavannes produced military watches for various armed forces during both World Wars, valued for their reliability and accuracy in field conditions.

name: Cortebert Watch Co
defunctReason: Cortebert was acquired by ETA SA in the 1960s, and the brand name was retired as production was folded into ETA's industrial movement manufacturing.
epitaph: Cortébert's railway chronometers kept Turkish and Yugoslav trains on time for decades — then ETA swallowed the factory whole.
description: Cortebert Watch Co was a Swiss manufacturer from the village of Cortébert in the Bernese Jura, known for producing robust railway chronometers supplied to state railways across Europe and the Middle East. Absorbed by ETA in the 1960s.

keyCollections.name: Railway Chronometer
keyCollections.description: Precision timekeepers supplied to state railways including Turkish State Railways (TCDD), Swiss Federal Railways, and various European and Middle Eastern railway operators, renowned for their accuracy and durability.

keyCollections.name: Grand Prix
keyCollections.description: Elegant dress watches that showcased Cortebert's ability to produce refined timepieces alongside their industrial chronometers, featuring clean dials and reliable movements.

keyCollections.name: Military Watches
keyCollections.description: Robust field watches supplied to various armed forces during the early-to-mid twentieth century, valued for their legibility and dependable movements.

timeline.event: Numa Jeannin-Simonin establishes a watch manufacturing operation in the village of Cortébert in the Bernese Jura.
The company is reorganised as Cortebert Watch Co and begins expanding production of precision movements.
Cortebert secures major contracts to supply railway chronometers to Turkish State Railways and other European railway operators.
The firm joins Ebauches SA, the Swiss movement manufacturing conglomerate, whilst retaining its brand identity.
Cortebert is absorbed into ETA SA as part of industry consolidation; movement production continues but branded watch output declines.
The Cortebert brand name is officially retired as operations are fully integrated into ETA's industrial movement manufacturing.

faqItems.question: When did Cortebert stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Cortebert ceased producing branded watches around 1970 when the company was fully absorbed into ETA SA, though the manufacturing facilities continued producing movements under the ETA name.

faqItems.question: Are Cortebert watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Vintage Cortebert watches, particularly railway chronometers and military pieces, are sought after by collectors for their historical significance and movement quality. Values vary considerably based on condition and provenance, with railway-issued examples commanding premiums.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Cortebert watch today?
faqItems.answer: Cortebert watches are only available on the vintage market, through specialist dealers, auction houses, and private sales. The brand has not been revived for new production.

faqItems.question: Why were Cortebert railway watches so highly regarded?
faqItems.answer: Cortebert developed a reputation for producing exceptionally accurate and robust chronometers that met the stringent timing requirements of railway operations. Their movements, particularly the Calibre 616 family, were prized for reliability in demanding conditions.

faqItems.question: What is the connection between Cortebert and ETA?
faqItems.answer: Cortebert joined Ebauches SA in 1932 and was eventually absorbed into ETA SA during the 1960s consolidation of the Swiss watch industry. The Cortebert name was retired, but the manufacturing expertise contributed to ETA's movement production.

name: Langendorf Watch Co (Lanco)
defunctReason: Langendorf, one of Switzerland's largest movement manufacturers, could not survive the quartz crisis and closed its Solothurn factory in the mid-1980s.
epitaph: Langendorf supplied movements to half of Switzerland — the factory that fed an industry starved when quartz killed the appetite.
description: Langendorf Watch Co, selling under the Lanco brand, was one of Switzerland's largest watch and movement manufacturers based in Langendorf, Solothurn. The company produced millions of movements annually and supplied calibres to numerous brands before the quartz crisis ended production.

keyCollections.name: Lanco Barracuda
keyCollections.description: A robust sports diver's watch from the 1960s and 1970s, featuring a rotating bezel and water resistance suitable for recreational diving.

keyCollections.name: Lanco Fon
keyCollections.description: An alarm wristwatch produced during the 1950s and 1960s, competing with similar complications from larger Swiss manufacturers.

keyCollections.name: Langendorf Military
keyCollections.description: Field watches supplied to various armed forces during the mid-twentieth century, known for legibility and durability under combat conditions.

keyCollections.name: Lanco Automatic
keyCollections.description: Post-war automatic timepieces using in-house calibres, offering Swiss reliability at accessible price points for everyday wear.

timeline.event: Adolf Haas establishes Langendorf Watch Co in the village of Langendorf, Canton Solothurn, initially focusing on movement manufacture.
The company expands significantly, becoming one of Switzerland's largest ébauche producers with substantial export volume.
Langendorf registers the Lanco trademark for finished watches sold under its own retail brand.
Post-war production peaks with millions of movements manufactured annually, supplying third-party brands across multiple continents.
The quartz crisis begins to erode demand for mechanical movements, forcing significant restructuring of operations.
Langendorf Watch Co ceases production and closes its Solothurn factory, unable to compete with Japanese quartz manufacturers.

faqItems.question: When did Langendorf (Lanco) stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Langendorf ceased all watch and movement production in 1985 when the company closed its factory in Langendorf, Solothurn, following years of declining demand during the quartz crisis.

faqItems.question: Are Langendorf and Lanco watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Vintage Lanco and Langendorf pieces remain modestly collectible, particularly military-issue watches and the Barracuda divers. Values are generally accessible compared to premium Swiss brands, making them attractive entry points for vintage collectors.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Lanco watch today?
faqItems.answer: New Lanco watches are no longer manufactured. However, vintage examples from the brand's extensive production history regularly appear at auction houses, vintage dealers, and online marketplaces.

faqItems.question: Did Langendorf make movements for other watch brands?
faqItems.answer: Yes, Langendorf was one of Switzerland's largest ébauche manufacturers, producing millions of movements annually that were sold to numerous watch brands who could not or chose not to produce their own calibres.

faqItems.question: What is the difference between Langendorf and Lanco?
faqItems.answer: Langendorf Watch Co was the manufacturing company name, whilst Lanco was the registered trademark used for finished watches sold directly to consumers. Both names appeared on dials depending on the market and era.

name: Excelsior Park
defunctReason: Excelsior Park was absorbed into the SSIH group and its chronograph movement production ceased as the Swatch Group consolidated Swiss manufacturing.
epitaph: The chronograph engine room of Saint-Imier — Excelsior Park movements powered Gallet, Girard-Perregaux, and a dozen others, always behind the curtain.
description: Excelsior Park was a Swiss chronograph movement manufacturer from Saint-Imier, founded in 1866. Its column-wheel chronograph calibres were used by Gallet, Girard-Perregaux, and many other brands. The manufacture was absorbed during Swiss industry consolidation.

keyCollections.name: Calibre 4 (EP4)
keyCollections.description: Excelsior Park's legendary column-wheel chronograph movement, prized for its precision and reliability, supplied to numerous prestigious watch houses throughout the twentieth century.

keyCollections.name: Calibre 40
keyCollections.description: A refined chronograph calibre that became widely adopted by brands seeking high-quality Swiss movement production during the mid-twentieth century.

keyCollections.name: Monte Carlo Chronograph
keyCollections.description: A branded chronograph wristwatch featuring Excelsior Park's own movements, notable for its racing-inspired aesthetics and robust construction.

keyCollections.name: Park 75
keyCollections.description: A later-generation chronograph calibre developed in the 1970s, representing the manufacture's continued innovation before industry consolidation.

timeline.event: Jules-Frédéric Jeanneret establishes Excelsior Park in Saint-Imier, initially producing watch components and movements.
The company begins specialising in chronograph movements, establishing its reputation for precision timing mechanisms.
Excelsior Park introduces the Calibre 4 (EP4), which becomes one of the most respected column-wheel chronograph movements in the industry.
The manufacture is integrated into the SSIH group alongside Omega and Tissot, continuing chronograph movement production.
Following the formation of the Swatch Group, Excelsior Park ceases independent production as manufacturing is consolidated.

faqItems.question: When did Excelsior Park stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Excelsior Park ceased independent movement production in 1985 following the consolidation of Swiss watch manufacturing under the newly formed Swatch Group, ending over a century of chronograph expertise.

faqItems.question: Are Excelsior Park watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Yes, Excelsior Park movements and branded chronographs are highly sought after by collectors. The EP4 calibre is particularly prized, and watches featuring these movements command premium prices at auction.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy an Excelsior Park watch today?
faqItems.answer: Excelsior Park watches and movements are available only through the vintage market, specialist dealers, and auction houses. The brand no longer produces timepieces.

faqItems.question: Which watch brands used Excelsior Park movements?
faqItems.answer: Numerous prestigious brands sourced Excelsior Park chronograph calibres, including Gallet, Girard-Perregaux, Universal Genève, and Heuer, among many others seeking high-quality column-wheel movements.

faqItems.question: What makes Excelsior Park chronograph movements special?
faqItems.answer: Excelsior Park movements are celebrated for their traditional column-wheel construction, exceptional finishing, and reliable performance, representing the finest Swiss chronograph manufacture traditions.

keyCollections.name: Calibre 170

Peak production period with Venus movements appearing in timepieces from over fifty different watch brands worldwide.
Venus SA acquired by Valjoux, with chronograph production consolidated and the Venus name subsequently discontinued.

faqItems.question: When did Venus stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Venus SA ceased independent operations in 1966 when it was acquired by Valjoux. The brand's chronograph movement production was absorbed into Valjoux's operations, and the Venus name was discontinued entirely.

faqItems.question: Are Venus watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Watches containing Venus movements, particularly the celebrated Calibre 175, remain highly collectible. Their value lies primarily in the historical significance of the movements rather than the Venus brand itself, as Venus supplied movements to numerous manufacturers.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Venus watch today?
faqItems.answer: Venus did not produce complete watches under its own name; it manufactured movements supplied to other brands. Vintage timepieces containing Venus calibres can be found through specialist dealers and auction houses, with examples from Breitling, Gallet, and other marques particularly sought after.

faqItems.question: Which watch brands used Venus movements?
faqItems.answer: Venus movements appeared in watches from dozens of manufacturers including Breitling, Gallet, Enicar, Wittnauer, Tissot, and many military contractors. The Calibre 175 alone was adopted by over fifty different brands during its production run.

faqItems.question: What happened to Venus after the Valjoux acquisition?
faqItems.answer: Following the 1966 acquisition, Venus's production facilities in Moutier were integrated into Valjoux's operations. Valjoux itself later became part of ETA SA, which today operates under the Swatch Group umbrella.

keyCollections.name: Calibre 51 Series

keyCollections.name: Calibre 248 Series

keyCollections.name: Calibre 149

faqItems.question: When did Landeron stop making watches?

faqItems.question: Are Landeron watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Landeron was an ébauche manufacturer rather than a finished watch brand, but vintage chronographs powered by Landeron movements remain highly collectible, particularly those featuring the popular Calibre 48 and 51 series.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Landeron watch today?
faqItems.answer: As Landeron produced movements rather than complete watches, collectors seek vintage timepieces from various brands that utilised Landeron calibres. These can be found through specialist dealers and auction houses.

faqItems.question: What brands used Landeron movements?
faqItems.answer: Landeron movements were used by numerous brands including Breitling, Wakmann, Bucherer, Olma, and many others who required affordable, reliable chronograph calibres for their timepieces.

faqItems.question: Why was Landeron so important to Swiss watchmaking?
faqItems.answer: Landeron democratised the chronograph complication by producing reliable, affordable movements that allowed smaller brands to offer chronograph watches without developing their own calibres.

faqItems.question: When did Ernest Borel stop making watches?

faqItems.question: Are Ernest Borel watches still valuable?

faqItems.question: Can I still buy an Ernest Borel watch today?

faqItems.question: Why was Ernest Borel called the 'honeymoon watch'?
faqItems.answer: Ernest Borel cultivated a romantic brand image in Chinese and Southeast Asian markets, positioning its watches as traditional wedding gifts symbolising eternal love, which earned it the affectionate nickname 'honeymoon watch' among generations of couples.

faqItems.question: What makes the Ernest Borel Cocktail special?
faqItems.answer: The Cocktail collection featured innovative dials with rotating inner discs that created ever-changing kaleidoscopic patterns, a technically playful and visually distinctive design that became the brand's most recognisable and collectible achievement.

keyCollections.name: Sowar Prima
keyCollections.description: The premium variant of the Sowar line, featuring higher-grade movements and refined finishing, often presented as gifts to mark significant life occasions.

keyCollections.name: Secundus

keyCollections.name: Queen Anne
keyCollections.description: An elegant dress watch collection that demonstrated the brand's versatility beyond utilitarian timepieces, popular among colonial administrators and merchants.

Ownership changes and declining investment led to reduced production quality and market presence.

faqItems.question: When did West End Watch Co stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: West End Watch Co ceased meaningful production around 2013, following decades of gradual decline from its peak prominence in the mid-20th century.

faqItems.question: Are West End Watch Co watches still valuable?

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a West End Watch Co watch today?

faqItems.question: Why was West End Watch Co so popular in India?

faqItems.question: What does 'Sowar' mean on West End watches?
faqItems.answer: Sowar is a Hindi and Urdu word meaning 'horseman' or 'cavalryman', reflecting the brand's strong military associations and its marketing to officers and soldiers across British India.

keyCollections.name: Dixieland
keyCollections.description: A range of robust, classically styled timepieces with automatic movements, offering accessible Swiss quality for everyday wear.

Auguste Reymond ceased production after 114 years, unable to sustain operations amid fierce competition in the mid-range Swiss watch segment.

faqItems.question: When did Auguste Reymond stop making watches?

faqItems.question: Are Auguste Reymond watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Auguste Reymond watches retain modest collector value, particularly the Art Deco-inspired Charleston and Jazz Age models. While not commanding premium prices, they are appreciated for their distinctive styling and Swiss craftsmanship.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy an Auguste Reymond watch today?
faqItems.answer: New Auguste Reymond watches are no longer available as the brand is defunct. However, pre-owned examples can be found through vintage watch dealers, auction houses, and online marketplaces at reasonable prices.

faqItems.question: What made Auguste Reymond watches distinctive?
faqItems.answer: The brand was known for its consistent Art Deco-inspired aesthetic, featuring rectangular and tonneau cases with elegant period styling. Their jazz-themed collection names reflected a unique brand identity celebrating the 1920s era.

faqItems.question: Where were Auguste Reymond watches made?
faqItems.answer: All Auguste Reymond watches were manufactured in Tramelan, a traditional watchmaking town in the Bernese Jura region of Switzerland, throughout the company's 114-year history.

keyCollections.name: Grade 910

keyCollections.name: Winnebago
keyCollections.description: A popular line named after the local Native American tribe, representing solid mid-grade movements for the general consumer market.

keyCollections.name: Grade 500 Series
keyCollections.description: Entry-level movements that made quality American watchmaking accessible to working-class buyers whilst maintaining respectable accuracy.

Rockford Watch Company declared bankruptcy and ceased operations, unable to sustain competition against larger manufacturers Elgin and Waltham.

faqItems.question: When did Rockford Watch Company stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Rockford Watch Company ceased production in 1915 when the firm declared bankruptcy, ending 42 years of American watchmaking after failing to compete with industry giants Elgin and Waltham.

faqItems.question: Are Rockford watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: High-grade Rockford movements, particularly the railroad-grade 900 and 910 series, remain sought after by collectors of American horology. Values depend significantly on grade, condition, and case material, with premium examples commanding respectable prices.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Rockford watch today?
faqItems.answer: Rockford watches are available only on the vintage and antique market, through specialist dealers, auctions, and private collectors. The brand has never been revived.

faqItems.question: Were Rockford watches used on American railroads?
faqItems.answer: Yes, Rockford produced movements that met railroad timing standards, particularly the Grade 900 and Grade 910 series with 21 jewels adjusted to five positions. These were approved for use by various railroad companies.

faqItems.question: How does Rockford quality compare to Elgin and Waltham?
faqItems.answer: Rockford's finest movements were considered equal in quality to the best offerings from Elgin and Waltham. The company's downfall was not quality but rather scale—they simply could not match the production volumes and marketing reach of their larger competitors.

keyCollections.name: Series XI

faqItems.question: When did E. Howard Watch Company stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: E. Howard ceased independent production in 1903 when acquired by Keystone Watch Case Company. The Howard name continued on watches of diminishing quality until approximately 1930, when production ended entirely.

faqItems.question: Are E. Howard watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Original E. Howard pocket watches, particularly those made before the 1903 Keystone acquisition, are highly valuable and prized by collectors. Pre-1903 examples in excellent condition can command significant prices, with rare models like the Edward Howard 23-jewel fetching thousands of pounds.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy an E. Howard watch today?
faqItems.answer: E. Howard watches can only be purchased on the secondary market through specialist dealers, auction houses, and collector networks. The brand has never been revived, making vintage examples the sole option for collectors.

faqItems.question: Why were E. Howard watches considered the finest American pocket watches?
faqItems.answer: E. Howard watches were renowned for their exceptional finishing, precise timekeeping, and stringent quality control. Edward Howard insisted on standards that rivalled Swiss manufacturers, and the company's movements became the benchmark for American railroad timing accuracy.

faqItems.question: What is the difference between pre-1903 and post-1903 Howard watches?
faqItems.answer: Pre-1903 Howard watches were manufactured in Boston under strict quality control and are considered true collector pieces. Post-1903 examples, produced under Keystone ownership, gradually declined in quality and are generally less valuable, though early Keystone-era pieces retain some collector interest.

faqItems.question: When did Columbus Watch Company stop making watches?

faqItems.question: Are Columbus Watch Company watches still valuable?

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Columbus Watch Company watch today?

faqItems.question: What is the connection between Columbus Watch Company and Gruen?

faqItems.question: What happened to Columbus Watch Company's machinery and tooling?

keyCollections.name: Crown

faqItems.question: When did New York Standard Watch Company stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: New York Standard Watch Company ceased operations in 1929, succumbing to bankruptcy during the economic instability that preceded the Great Depression. The company had struggled to maintain profitability in an increasingly competitive market for affordable timepieces.

faqItems.question: Are New York Standard Watch Company watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: New York Standard watches hold modest value among collectors of American horology, typically fetching between £30 and £200 depending on condition and model. faqItems.question: Can I still buy a New York Standard Watch Company watch today?
faqItems.answer: Vintage New York Standard pocket watches can be found through antique dealers, estate sales, and online auction platforms. faqItems.question: What made the worm-gear mechanism distinctive?

faqItems.question: Who bought New York Standard watches when they were new?
faqItems.answer: The company specifically targeted working-class Americans who needed affordable, functional timepieces. Factory workers, farmers, and tradesmen comprised the primary customer base, as these watches cost significantly less than offerings from premium American manufacturers.

faqItems.question: When did Seth Thomas stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Seth Thomas Watch Company ceased watch production around 1915. The parent clock company determined that competing against established watch manufacturers was not economically viable and chose to concentrate on its dominant position in the American clock market.

faqItems.question: Are Seth Thomas watches still valuable?

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Seth Thomas watch today?

faqItems.question: What made Maiden Lane watches special?
faqItems.answer: The Maiden Lane series represented Seth Thomas's finest work, featuring precision-adjusted movements, gold jewel settings, elaborately damaskeened plates, and construction quality that rivalled contemporary high-grade movements from Waltham and Elgin.

faqItems.question: Why is the brand named Seth Thomas?
faqItems.answer: The watch company took its name from its parent organisation, the Seth Thomas Clock Company, which was itself named after clockmaker Seth Thomas (1785–1859), one of the pioneers of American clockmaking who had founded the clock business in 1813.

faqItems.question: When did Trenton Watch Company stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Trenton ceased independent production in 1908 when it was acquired by Ingersoll. The factory continued operating under Ingersoll ownership, producing movements for the famous dollar watches, but the Trenton brand identity was discontinued.

faqItems.question: Are Trenton watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Trenton pocket watches hold modest value among American horology collectors. faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Trenton watch today?

faqItems.question: What happened to the Trenton factory after the Ingersoll acquisition?
faqItems.answer: The Trenton facility became instrumental in Ingersoll's success, manufacturing the movements that powered millions of dollar watches. This factory enabled Ingersoll to meet enormous demand for affordable timepieces in the early twentieth century.

faqItems.question: Why was Trenton significant in American watchmaking history?
faqItems.answer: Trenton represented the American watchmaking industry's push to produce affordable, domestically manufactured timepieces. Its acquisition by Ingersoll exemplified the consolidation occurring in the industry, ultimately contributing to the mass production of watches accessible to ordinary Americans.

epitaph: They solved magnetism before anyone else cared — Non-Magnetic's palladium alloy hairsprings were a century ahead of their time.
description: Non-Magnetic Watch Company of America was a fascinating Swiss-American venture, manufacturing movements in Geneva with palladium alloy balance springs resistant to magnetism. The company's innovations predated modern anti-magnetic watchmaking by a century.

keyCollections.name: Paillard Non-Magnetic
keyCollections.description: The flagship collection featuring palladium alloy hairsprings and balance wheels, specifically engineered to resist magnetic interference—a revolutionary concept in the 1880s.

keyCollections.name: 18-Size Railroad Grade
keyCollections.description: Full-plate movements designed to meet the exacting standards of American railroad timekeeping, combining non-magnetic properties with precision regulation.

timeline.event: Non-Magnetic Watch Company of America founded, establishing manufacturing operations in Geneva, Switzerland, whilst maintaining commercial headquarters in New York.

The company exhibited at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, demonstrating the magnetic resistance of their timepieces.
Financial restructuring occurred following patent litigation and increasing competition from established American manufacturers.
The Non-Magnetic Watch Company ceased operations following prolonged financial difficulties and unresolved patent disputes.

faqItems.question: When did Non-Magnetic Watch Company stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: The Non-Magnetic Watch Company ceased production around 1905, approximately eighteen years after its founding, due to a combination of patent disputes and financial difficulties.

faqItems.question: Are Non-Magnetic Watch Company watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Yes, particularly among collectors of American horological history. Their pioneering use of palladium alloys for non-magnetic properties makes them historically significant, and well-preserved examples command premium prices at auction.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Non-Magnetic Watch Company watch today?
faqItems.answer: Original Non-Magnetic Watch Company timepieces can only be found on the secondary market through specialist dealers, auction houses, and collector networks. The brand has never been revived.

faqItems.question: Why was non-magnetic technology important in the 1880s?
faqItems.answer: The proliferation of electrical equipment and telegraph systems in the late 19th century meant that railroad workers and electrical engineers faced increasing magnetic interference with their timepieces. Non-Magnetic Watch Company addressed this practical problem decades before it became an industry standard.

faqItems.question: Where were Non-Magnetic Watch Company movements actually made?
faqItems.answer: Despite the American company name, the movements were manufactured in Geneva, Switzerland, utilising Swiss craftsmanship whilst incorporating Paillard's patented non-magnetic alloys. This Swiss-American arrangement was unusual for the period.

Financial difficulties mounted as the company struggled with undercapitalisation despite producing quality timepieces.
Company declared bankruptcy after eight years of operation; assets and machinery subsequently acquired for use by other manufacturers.

faqItems.question: When did United States Watch Company (Marion) stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: The company ceased production in 1872 when it declared bankruptcy, having operated for only eight years despite producing well-regarded timepieces.

faqItems.question: Are United States Watch Company (Marion) watches still valuable?
faqItems.answer: Yes, Marion watches are prized by collectors of early American horology. Higher grades such as the George Channing and Fayette Stratton command premium prices due to their quality and historical significance.

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a United States Watch Company (Marion) watch today?
faqItems.answer: Original Marion watches can be found through antique dealers, auction houses, and specialist horological collectors. Given the company's brief existence, surviving examples are relatively scarce.

faqItems.question: Why did the United States Watch Company of Marion fail?
faqItems.answer: The company was undercapitalised from the outset and struggled to compete with established manufacturers. Post-Civil War economic conditions and the costs of establishing a new factory proved insurmountable.

faqItems.question: What happened to the Marion factory equipment after bankruptcy?
faqItems.answer: The machinery and tooling were sold and subsequently used by other American watch companies, ensuring the technical innovations developed at Marion continued to influence the industry.

faqItems.question: When did Helbros stop making watches?
faqItems.answer: Helbros ceased operations in approximately 1995, having struggled throughout the 1980s and early 1990s against inexpensive Asian quartz imports that undercut its position in the American fashion watch market.

faqItems.question: Are Helbros watches still valuable?

faqItems.question: Can I still buy a Helbros watch today?
faqItems.answer: New Helbros watches are no longer manufactured. However, vintage examples remain readily available through online auction sites, estate sales, and specialist vintage watch dealers.

faqItems.question: Were Helbros watches made in America or Switzerland?
faqItems.answer: Helbros used Swiss-made movements imported to their New York headquarters, where watches were assembled and cased. This practice was common among American watch brands seeking to combine Swiss precision with domestic marketing and distribution.

faqItems.question: Why was Helbros so popular in mid-century America?
faqItems.answer: Helbros succeeded through aggressive department store distribution, affordable pricing, and stylish designs that appealed to everyday Americans. The brand offered Swiss-quality movements at accessible prices, positioning itself between cheap domestic alternatives and expensive luxury imports.

Following the quartz crisis, the brand began licensing its name for increasingly lower-quality products.
